assessment: Finish the required labs in each module: they are checked automatically and explained when something is missing.
Pass each module quiz (70% or more). You can retry as often as you like.
Complete the sales analysis, the memo and the final assessment to finish the course.

faq.a: No. The labs run in an in-browser spreadsheet that supports the functions this course uses, including SUMIFS, STDEV.S, QUARTILE, FORECAST and NORM.S.DIST.

faq.q: Does it cover Power Query, PivotTables and Power Pivot?
faq.a: They are explained and mapped to the formulas that do the same job, so you understand what they do. They run only in desktop Excel and Power BI, so there is no hands-on lab for them here.
Basic formulas such as SUM, AVERAGE and IF. If you are new to Excel, start with Basic Microsoft Excel.
About 22 hours at a relaxed pace, in short sessions.
Finishing every module and the final assessment marks the course complete on your Yugty profile.

activities.title: Clean the customer list
activities.objective: Turn messy names and text amounts into clean names and real numbers using formulas.
activities.scenario: An export gives customer names with stray spaces and wrong capitals, and amounts typed as text such as 'Rs 1200'. Clean both in helper columns and total the amounts.
steps: In B2 clean the name with PROPER(TRIM(A2)), then copy the same formula down to B6.
In D2 remove the 'Rs ' prefix with SUBSTITUTE and convert the result with VALUE, then fill down to D6.
In D7 add the five amounts with SUM.

checks.label: B2 shows Asha Rao
checks.explain: TRIM removes the extra spaces first, then PROPER capitalises each word.

checks.label: B3 shows Bilal Khan (extra spaces inside the name removed)
checks.hint: Copy the formula from B2 to B3.
checks.explain: TRIM also removes repeated spaces between words.

checks.label: B6 shows Esha Gupta
checks.hint: Fill the formula down to row 6.
checks.explain: Every row needs its own formula pointing at its own raw name.

checks.label: D2 is the number 1200
checks.explain: SUBSTITUTE removes the text prefix; VALUE turns what is left into a real number.

checks.label: D5 is the number 400
checks.hint: Fill the formula down to row 5.
checks.explain: The same pattern works for every row.

checks.label: D7 totals the amounts to 6,500
checks.explain: SUM only adds real numbers, so a total of 6,500 proves the text became numbers.

checks.label: No error messages
checks.hint: If you see #VALUE!, check the exact text you remove in SUBSTITUTE (it includes a space).
checks.explain: Errors usually come from a reference or text that does not match.

activities.title: Dates and weekdays
activities.objective: Take dates apart and measure the time between them.
activities.scenario: Orders carry a date. The warehouse wants the month and weekday of each order, and the number of days left until 1 April 2025.
steps: In B2 show the month as text with TEXT(A2,"mmm"), then fill down.
In C2 show the weekday with TEXT(A2,"dddd"), then fill down.
In D2 subtract the order date from DATE(2025,4,1) to get the days left, then fill down.

checks.label: B2 shows Jan
checks.explain: The format code mmm shows a three-letter month name.

checks.label: C3 shows Monday (3 February 2025)
checks.explain: dddd shows the full weekday name.

checks.label: C4 shows Friday
checks.explain: 28 February 2025 was a Friday.

checks.label: D2 is 76 days
checks.explain: Dates are numbers underneath, so subtracting gives the days between.

checks.label: D6 is 1 day
checks.hint: Fill the formula down to row 6.
checks.explain: 31 March is one day before 1 April.

checks.label: No error messages
checks.hint: Check that each date is typed as year-month-day.
checks.explain: ISO dates (2025-03-09) are understood by every function.

activities.title: Profile the daily sales
activities.objective: Describe a column: centre, spread, quartiles and outliers.
activities.scenario: Twelve days of unit sales are in A2:A13, and one day looks unusually high. Build the profile: the mean, median, mode, sample standard deviation, quartiles, interquartile range, the upper fence of the IQR rule, and how many days exceed that fence.
steps: Fill E2 to E7 with AVERAGE, MEDIAN, MODE, STDEV.S, and the first and third QUARTILE of A2:A13.
In E8 subtract Q1 from Q3 to get the IQR, and in E9 add 1.5 times the IQR to Q3 for the upper fence.
In E10 count the days above the fence with COUNTIF(A2:A13,">"&E9).

checks.label: The mean is about 27.08
checks.explain: The mean adds all values and divides by how many there are; the one high day lifts it.

checks.label: The median is 21
checks.explain: The middle two sorted values are both 21, so the median is not affected by the high day.

checks.label: The mode is 22 (four values tie at two days; MODE returns the first one in the list)
checks.explain: MODE returns the value that appears most often. When several tie, it returns the one that appears first in the data.

checks.label: The sample standard deviation is about 21.77
checks.explain: STDEV.S measures the typical distance from the mean; the high day makes it large.

checks.label: Q1 is 19.75
checks.explain: A quarter of the days are below this value.

checks.label: Q3 is 22.25
checks.explain: Three quarters of the days are below this value.

checks.label: The IQR is 2.5
checks.explain: The IQR is Q3 minus Q1, the spread of the middle half.

checks.label: The upper fence is 26
checks.explain: Values above Q3 plus 1.5 times the IQR are flagged as outliers.

checks.label: One day is above the fence
checks.explain: Only the 96 exceeds 26.

activities.title: Build a histogram
activities.objective: Count values into bins with COUNTIFS and chart the result.
activities.scenario: Twenty order values (in rupees) are in A2:A21. Count how many fall into each of four bins and chart the counts. The counts should add up to 20.
steps: In G2 count the values that are at least the lower bound (E2) and below the upper bound (F2) with COUNTIFS.
Copy the formula down to G5. Use $A$2:$A$21 so the data range does not slide.
In G6 add the four counts and check that you get 20.
Insert a bar chart of the counts (labels D2:D5, values G2:G5).

checks.label: The first bin counts 9 orders
checks.explain: Two conditions give a lower and an upper bound: at least 0 and below 100.

checks.label: The second bin counts 6 orders
checks.hint: Copy the formula down; E3 and F3 are the bounds.
checks.explain: Each bin has its own lower and upper bound.

checks.label: The third bin counts 3 orders
checks.hint: Copy the formula down to row 4.
checks.explain: Values from 200 up to but not including 300.

checks.label: The last bin counts 2 orders
checks.hint: Copy the formula down to row 5.
checks.explain: The last bin has a very high upper bound so it catches everything above 300.

checks.label: The counts add up to 20
checks.explain: If the total is not 20, a bin boundary overlaps or leaves a gap.

checks.label: A bar chart of the counts exists
checks.hint: Use the chart button, choose a bar chart, labels D2:D5 and values G2:G5.
checks.explain: A histogram is a column chart of counts per bin.

activities.title: Compare two exam scores
activities.objective: Use z-scores to compare values on different scales.
activities.scenario: Anil scored 78 in a test with mean 70 and standard deviation 8. Beena scored 85 in a test with mean 80 and standard deviation 10. Who did better compared with their own class?
steps: In B5 compute Anil's z-score with STANDARDIZE(B2,B3,B4), and in C5 do the same for Beena.
In B6 convert each z-score to a percentile with NORM.S.DIST(z, TRUE).
In B7 write 'Anil' or 'Beena' for whoever has the higher percentile, using IF.

checks.label: Anil's z-score is 1
checks.explain: z = (78 - 70) / 8 = 1: one standard deviation above his class mean.

checks.label: Anil's percentile is about 0.841
checks.explain: A z-score of 1 sits at about the 84th percentile of a bell curve.

checks.label: Beena's percentile is about 0.691
checks.explain: A z-score of 0.5 sits at about the 69th percentile.

checks.label: B7 names Anil
checks.explain: Compare the percentiles, not the raw scores.

activities.title: Region by product cross-tab
activities.objective: Build a cross-tab with one SUMIFS formula that uses mixed references.
activities.scenario: Ten sales rows are in A2:D11. Build a cross-tab of revenue by region (down the side) and product (across the top), with totals.
steps: In G2 write SUMIFS with $D$2:$D$11 as the values, region criteria $F2 and product criteria G$1.
Copy it across to H2 and down to row 4 without changing it.
Add the row totals in I2:I4, the column totals in G5:H5, and the grand total in I5.

checks.label: G2 is North Pen revenue: 180
checks.explain: SUMIFS adds revenue where the region matches the row label and the product matches the column heading.

spec.patternMsg: Use $F2 for the region and G$1 for the product, so the formula can be copied across the grid.

checks.label: H2 is North Book revenue: 400
checks.explain: Copying right moves G$1 to H$1, which picks up Book.

spec.patternMsg: Copy the same formula from G2 so the references stay mixed.

checks.label: G3 is South Pen revenue: 260
checks.explain: Copying down moves $F2 to $F3, which picks up South.

checks.label: H4 is East Book revenue: 200
checks.hint: Copy the formula to the bottom right cell.
checks.explain: Each cell of the grid has its own region and product.

checks.label: I2 is the North row total: 580
checks.explain: A row total adds the products for one region.

checks.label: G5 is the Pen column total: 630
checks.explain: A column total adds the regions for one product.

checks.label: I5 is the grand total: 1,330, the same as the source column
checks.explain: The grand total must equal the sum of the source data: if it does not, a category is missing or misspelled.

activities.title: Pareto of products
activities.objective: Calculate share, cumulative share and an A/B/C class.
activities.scenario: Products are already sorted by revenue, largest first. Find which few products make up most of the revenue.
steps: In B9 add the revenues. In C2 divide each product's revenue by the total ($B$9) and fill down.
In D2 the cumulative share starts equal to the share; from D3 add the share to the cumulative above.
In E2 classify: A while the cumulative share is up to 80%, B up to 95%, otherwise C.

checks.label: B9 is the total revenue: 1,300
checks.explain: The total is the denominator for every share.

checks.label: C2 is the Laptop share: 40%
checks.explain: Lock the total with $B$9 so it does not slide when you copy the formula down.

spec.patternMsg: Lock the total with $B$9 so every row divides by the same number.

checks.label: C5 is the Watch share: about 9.2%
checks.explain: 120 divided by 1,300.

checks.label: D3 is the cumulative share of the top two: about 63.8%
checks.explain: The cumulative share adds each share to the running total above it.

checks.label: D8 reaches 100%
checks.hint: Fill the cumulative formula down to row 8.
checks.explain: The last cumulative share is always 100%.

checks.label: E4 classifies Tablet as A
checks.explain: Tablet's cumulative share is 78.5%, within the first 80%.

checks.label: E6 classifies Earbuds as B
checks.explain: 94.6% is above 80% and up to 95%.

checks.label: E8 classifies Case as C
checks.hint: Fill the class formula down to row 8.
checks.explain: Anything beyond 95% cumulative is class C.

activities.title: The conversion-rate trap
activities.objective: Calculate an overall rate as a ratio of totals, and see why averaging rates is wrong.
activities.scenario: Three channels bring visitors and orders. The channel rates are 5%, 10% and 20%. What is the real overall conversion rate?
steps: In D2 to D4 divide orders by visits for each channel.
In D6 do the wrong thing on purpose: the average of the three rates.
In D7 do it right: total orders divided by total visits.

checks.label: D2 is Email's rate: 5%
checks.explain: Orders divided by visits.

checks.label: D4 is Social's rate: 20%
checks.explain: 10 divided by 50.

checks.label: D6 averages the three rates (about 11.7%)
checks.explain: This gives each channel equal weight, even though Email has most of the visitors.

checks.label: D7 is total orders over total visits: 6.4%
checks.explain: Add the numerators and the denominators first, then divide once: 80 / 1,250.

activities.title: Ads and sales: fit a line
activities.objective: Measure a relationship and use it to predict.
activities.scenario: Six months of advertising spend (₹ thousand) and sales (₹ lakh) are in A2:B7. Measure the relationship and predict the sales for a spend of 70.
steps: In E2 find the correlation with CORREL(B2:B7,A2:A7), and in E3 the R squared with RSQ.
In E4 and E5 find the slope and the intercept of sales on spend.
In E6 forecast the sales for a spend of 70 with FORECAST(70,B2:B7,A2:A7) and in E7 check it equals the intercept plus the slope times 70.

checks.label: The correlation is about 0.994
checks.explain: The points lie close to a rising straight line.

checks.label: R squared is about 0.989
checks.explain: R squared is the correlation squared: the share of the variation the line explains.

checks.label: The slope is about 0.946
checks.explain: Each extra ₹1 thousand of ads goes with about ₹0.95 lakh more sales.

checks.label: The intercept is about 1.73
checks.explain: The line's value when the spend is 0.

checks.label: The forecast for a spend of 70 is about 67.93
checks.explain: Put the new x first, then known y values, then known x values.

checks.label: E7 rebuilds the forecast from the slope and intercept
checks.explain: FORECAST is just intercept plus slope times x.

activities.title: Smooth the series and find the seasons
activities.objective: Build a moving average and a seasonal index.
activities.scenario: Twelve months of sales are in B2:B13. Smooth them with a 3-month moving average, and measure each month against the yearly average with a seasonal index.
steps: In C4 average the latest three months with AVERAGE(B2:B4) and fill down to C13.
In B14 find the average month with AVERAGE(B2:B13).
In D2 divide each month by the average ($B$14) and fill down: that is the seasonal index.

checks.label: C4 averages Jan to Mar: 133.3
checks.explain: The first moving average needs three months, so it starts in March.

checks.label: C8 averages May to Jul: 196.7
checks.hint: Fill the formula down: each row averages its own and the two months above.
checks.explain: The window moves one month at a time.

checks.label: C13 averages Oct to Dec: 130
checks.hint: Fill the formula down to row 13.

checks.label: B14 is the average month: 158.3
checks.explain: The seasonal index divides each month by this average.

checks.label: June's seasonal index is about 1.33
checks.explain: 210 / 158.3: June is about a third above an average month.

spec.patternMsg: Lock the average with $B$14 so every month divides by the same number.

checks.label: December's seasonal index is about 0.63
checks.explain: 100 / 158.3: December is well below an average month.

activities.title: Break-even and scenarios
activities.objective: Build a small model with inputs, then compute break-even, profit under three scenarios and the margin of safety.
activities.scenario: A product sells for ₹500, costs ₹300 per unit to make, and has ₹200,000 of fixed costs. Sales could be 800 units (worst), 1,200 (base) or 1,600 (best). Use only the input cells in your formulas.
steps: In B5 compute the contribution per unit (price minus variable cost) and in B6 the break-even units.
In C9:C11 compute the profit for each scenario from its units (B9:B11).
In B13 compute the margin of safety for the base case: units above break-even divided by base units.

checks.label: B5 (contribution) is 200
checks.explain: Each unit contributes the price minus its variable cost toward fixed costs.

checks.label: B6 (break-even) is 1,000 units
checks.explain: Fixed costs divided by the contribution per unit.

checks.label: C9 is the worst-case profit: -40,000
checks.explain: 800 units earn 160,000, which does not cover 200,000 of fixed costs.

checks.label: C10 is the base-case profit: 40,000
checks.hint: Copy the formula down, using each scenario's units.

checks.label: C11 is the best-case profit: 120,000
checks.hint: Copy the formula down to row 11.

checks.label: B13 (margin of safety) is about 16.7%
checks.explain: The base volume is 200 above break-even, which is a sixth of 1,200.

activities.title: Test an A/B result
activities.objective: Decide whether a difference in conversion rates is statistically significant.
activities.scenario: Version A converted 120 of 2,400 visitors; version B converted 150 of 2,500. B looks better. Is the difference big enough to rule out chance?
steps: In B4 and C4 compute each version's rate. In B5 compute the pooled rate: all conversions divided by all visitors.
In B6 compute the standard error: SQRT(pooled × (1 − pooled) × (1/visitorsA + 1/visitorsB)).
In B7 compute z = (rate B − rate A) / standard error. In B8 compute the two-sided p-value: 2*(1-NORM.S.DIST(ABS(z),TRUE)).
In B9 write 'Significant' if the p-value is below 0.05, otherwise 'Not significant'.

checks.label: B4 is A's rate: 5%
checks.explain: Conversions divided by visitors.

checks.label: C4 is B's rate: 6%
checks.explain: The same calculation for version B.

checks.label: B5 is the pooled rate: about 5.5%
checks.explain: If there were no real difference, the best estimate of the rate is all conversions over all visitors.

checks.label: B6 is the standard error: about 0.00652
checks.explain: It measures how much a difference between two such samples would wobble by chance.

checks.label: B7 is z: about 1.53
checks.explain: The observed difference, in standard errors.

checks.label: B8 is the p-value: about 0.125
checks.explain: The chance of seeing a gap at least this large if the versions were really equal.

checks.label: B9 says Not significant
checks.explain: A p-value of 0.125 is above 0.05: the data does not show B is reliably better.

activities.title: Choose a supplier by weighted score
activities.objective: Compare options with weights, and check the ranking is robust.
activities.scenario: Three suppliers are scored from 1 to 10 on cost, quality and speed. Cost weighs 40%, quality 35% and speed 25%. Which supplier wins?
steps: In E2 compute supplier A's weighted score with SUMPRODUCT(B2:D2,$B$6:$D$6) and fill down to E4.
In B8 name the best supplier using INDEX and MATCH on the highest score.

checks.label: E2 is A's score: 7.1
checks.explain: SUMPRODUCT multiplies each score by its weight and adds them.

spec.patternMsg: Lock the weights with $B$6:$D$6 so they do not slide when you fill down.

checks.label: E4 is C's score: 7.8
checks.hint: Fill the formula down to row 4.

checks.label: B8 names supplier C
checks.explain: MATCH finds the position of the highest score and INDEX returns the supplier name in that position.

activities.title: Build a KPI dashboard
activities.objective: Compute KPI cards with a target comparison and a status, and chart the trend.
activities.scenario: Monthly revenue for six months is in B2:B7 with a target of 100,000 a month. Build three KPI cards (total revenue, best month, average vs target) with a status, and a chart.
steps: In E2 total the revenue and in E3 find the best month's value with MAX. In E4 find the best month's name with INDEX and MATCH.
In E5 compute the average month as a percentage of the target (D1) and in E6 give a status: 'On track' at 100% or more, 'Watch' from 90%, otherwise 'Behind'.
